source: The Lorentz Force
F = q(E + v × B), computed with cross products.
Students take v × B in the wrong order, or forget that a negative charge feels the opposite force.

In Physics 2 the magnetic force had a size, $qvB\sin\theta$, and a direction from the right-hand rule. The cross product packs both into one operation, and adding the electric force gives the complete force on a charge in any fields.

The Lorentz force: $$\role{force}{\vec{F}} = \role{charge}{q}\left(\role[electric field]{field}{\vec{E}} + \role{velocity}{\vec{v}}\times\role[magnetic field]{field}{\vec{B}}\right),$$ $$\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = \left(v_yB_z - v_zB_y,\ \ v_zB_x - v_xB_z,\ \ v_xB_y - v_yB_x\right).$$ For a negative charge, $q < 0$ reverses the force.

A cross product has exactly the properties the magnetic force has: its size is $vB\sin\theta$ (zero when $\vec{v}$ runs along $\vec{B}$, largest when they are perpendicular), and it points perpendicular to both $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$. Because the magnetic part is always perpendicular to $\vec{v}$, it does no work: $\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = 0$. A magnetic field can bend a charge's path but never speed it up or slow it down.
A charge entering a uniform field at $60^\circ$. The part of $\vec{v}$ along $\vec{B}$ feels nothing; the part across $\vec{B}$ is turned into a circle. Together they make a helix.
$\vec{v} = (3, 0, -1)$ and $\vec{B} = (0, 2, 5)$ from the first example, with $\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ perpendicular to both. Turn the view to check.
Worked examples
A $+2.0\ \mu\text{C}$ charge moves with $\vec{v} = (3, 0, -1) \times 10^{3}\ \text{m/s}$ in $\vec{B} = (0, 0.2, 0.5)\ \text{T}$. Find $\vec{F}$.
Force from components
Factor out the scales: $\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = (10^3)(0.1)\,\big[(3, 0, -1)\times(0, 2, 5)\big]$.
Show that the force in the first example is perpendicular to the velocity.
Checking that it does no work
$\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = 0$
Zero, as it must be: the magnetic force changes only the direction of motion.
An electron moves along $+x$ through a field along $+z$. Which way is the force?
An electron's direction
$\hat{\imath}\times\hat{k} = -\hat{\jmath}$, so $\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ points along $-y$.
The electron's charge is negative, which flips it: the force points along $+y$.

Nature uses this all the time. Charged particles streaming from the Sun meet Earth's magnetic field and spiral along its field lines, which funnel them toward the polar regions; where they strike the upper atmosphere, it glows as the aurora.

Taking $\vec{B}\times\vec{v}$ instead of $\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$, or forgetting the charge's sign. Swapping the order reverses a cross product, and so does a negative charge; doing either by accident gives a force pointing exactly backward. Two checks: the force must be perpendicular to both $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$ (dot products zero), and for a proton moving along $+x$ in a field along $+y$ the force is along $+z$ ($\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\jmath} = \hat{k}$).
